newsitem.title: USA: Wall Street seen rising at the open.
newsitem.headline: Wall Street seen rising at the open.

text.p: Wall Street shares are expected to open higher Wednesday, taking momentum from yesterday's powerful rise and from end-of-quarter portfolio adjustments by money managers, analysts said.

Investors will be watching for May durable goods orders and existing home sales data, due today, but analysts said the figures would have to be much stronger than expected to dampen market enthusiasm.
"The rally looks set to resume," said Peter Cardillo, director of research at Westfalia Investments.
The Dow Jones Industrial Average rebounded on Tuesday, erasing nearly all of Monday's steep losses to finish up 153.80 points at 7758.06.
This morning the Standard & Poor's 500 futures index was off 0.50 point at 904.50.

"Despite the fact that the futures are off slightly, I think we're set for a higher open," said Thom Brown, managing director of Rutherford Brown and Catherwood. "Some stocks are higher in London and...there's not much to stand in the market's way."
Large-capitalization stocks, which have been consistent strong performers, are expected to be the focus of buying interest as the quarter draws to a close, analysts said.
"We should see switching as we approach the end of the second quarter," Cardillo said. "Money managers will be looking to get back into high-quality big name issues which they might have sold."
Drug, financial and large-cap technology stocks are among those seen leading the broader market up, he said.
Tobacco stocks will also draw attention as more details emerge on the tobacco industry settlement.

Philip Morris Cos Inc is expected to provide $6.5 billion of the initial $10 billion payment called for from the tobacco industry under the accord between cigarette makers and U.S. states, the New York Times reported. RJR Nabisco Holdings Corp said it expected its initial payment would be $600 million.
Durable goods orders for May are due at 0830 EDT/1230 GMT, and a sharp rise could send bonds and stocks lower.
"But (the rise) would have to be really dramatic to offset the PPI and CPI, which are the best inflation news we've had since 1953," Brown said.
Durable goods orders are forecast to rise 0.6 percent.
May existing home sales data, due at 1000 EDT/1400 EDT, are forecast at an annual rate of 4.07 million.
Japan's Nikkei average closed up 337.34 points at 20,679.27.
In London the FTSE 100 was up 41.1 points at 4637.4.
U.S. stocks trading in London were mostly flat. But some issues, including Dow components Philip Morris and Boeing Co, were firm.
The long bond was down 12/32 at a 6.72 percent yield.

The dollar fell against the yen after the Bank of Japan's "Tankan Survey" showed a strong improvement in business sentiment. The dollar was trading at 113.50/60 yen in Tokyo and at 1.7233/38 marks in Europe.
The Wall Street Journal said in its Heard on the Street column that many analysts think investment bank Donaldson, Lufkin & Jenrette is an attractive takeover target.
The New York Times said in its Market Place column that the Hong Kong stock market is seeing record highs and volume just days before Britain hands Hong Kong over to China.
((--Wall Street Desk 212-859-1730))
